## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. use CorelDRAW tools to plan and build a design for a client;
2. explain RGB and CMYK colour and say which is for screen and which for print;
3. calculate the print size of a picture from its pixels and resolution;
4. choose a suitable file format for a purpose.

## Materials

Computers with CorelDRAW (or Inkscape), a projector, a printed full-colour flyer, a calculator, sample files in .cdr, .jpg, .png and .pdf.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show a flyer on the projector and on paper. Ask: why do the colours look brighter on the screen than on paper? Collect answers.

## Development

1. Recap vector and bitmap graphics and the CorelDRAW tools. A design for a client begins with a brief: purpose, size, text, colours.
2. Colour models: RGB (red, green, blue) is for screens; CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow, black) is for printing. Printing from RGB can dull the colours.
3. Resolution: pixels per inch (dpi or ppi). Print size = pixels / dpi. Work: 1,200 x 900 pixels at 300 dpi = 4 x 3 inches. Pictures for print need about 300 dpi; for screens 72 to 96 are enough.
4. File formats: .cdr (editable CorelDRAW), JPEG (photographs, small, loses some quality), PNG (graphics with clear backgrounds), PDF (for printing and sharing).
5. Good design: alignment, contrast, a few fonts, and space between items.

## Class activity

Pupils plan a one-page flyer for a school quiz: size, text, colours and format for printing.

## Evaluation

1. Which colour model is used for printing?
2. A picture is 1,500 pixels wide at 300 dpi. How wide will it print?

Complete the problem set and the worksheet on the app.

# Graphic design in practice: colour, resolution and file formats

## From brief to design

A designer starts with a **brief**: who it is for, what it must say, its size and where it will be shown. A flyer for a school quiz needs a title, date, venue and one clear picture. The designer sketches the layout, then builds it in a package such as CorelDRAW with the rectangle, ellipse and text tools, and the fill and outline tools.

## Colour models

- **RGB (red, green, blue)** mixes light and is used for screens: phones, monitors and projectors.
- **CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow, black)** mixes inks and is used for printing.

A design for print should be set up in CMYK, so the colours you see are close to those that will be printed. Very bright screen colours may look duller on paper.

## Resolution and print size

**Resolution** is the number of pixels in each inch, called **dpi** (dots per inch) or ppi. For good printing a picture needs about **300 dpi**; for a screen, **72 to 96 dpi** is enough.

**Print size = number of pixels divided by dpi.**

**Worked example.** A photograph is 1,200 pixels wide and 900 pixels high. At 300 dpi, width = 1,200 / 300 = **4 inches** and height = 900 / 300 = **3 inches**. If you stretch the same picture to 8 inches wide, the resolution falls to 1,200 / 8 = 150 dpi and the print looks blurred.

## File formats

| Format | Use |
| --- | --- |
| .cdr | the editable CorelDRAW design |
| JPEG (.jpg) | photographs; small file but loses some quality |
| PNG (.png) | graphics with a clear background such as logos on web pages |
| PDF (.pdf) | sharing and printing, keeps the layout |

Always keep the .cdr file so you can edit the design later, and export the other formats.

## Rules of good design

Keep **alignment** tidy, use strong **contrast** between text and background, limit yourself to two or three **fonts**, leave **white space**, and place the most important item first.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. explain why a computer must be maintained and distinguish preventive from corrective maintenance;
2. clean a computer, and charge and replace batteries and UPS safely;
3. list hardware and software maintenance tasks;
4. explain what a computer crash is and how data is recovered.

## Materials

A soft brush, a dry cloth, screen wipes, an air blower, a UPS, a laptop battery, a DVD drive with a lens cleaning disc, a flash drive with a backup.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: your family's generator needs servicing every few months. Does a computer need servicing too? What goes wrong when it is never cleaned or updated?

## Development

1. Maintenance keeps a computer working. Preventive maintenance is done regularly to stop faults; corrective maintenance repairs a fault after it occurs.
2. General cleaning: switch off and unplug first; dust the case with a soft brush; wipe the screen with a slightly damp soft cloth; clean the keyboard with an air blower; never spray liquid directly.
3. Batteries: charge a laptop battery before it is fully empty, avoid overheating, and replace a swollen or faulty battery. A UPS battery lasts about three to five years and is replaced when it cannot hold a charge.
4. DVD drive: clean the lens with a lens cleaning disc.
5. Hardware tasks: check cables, fans and the power supply. Software tasks: update the operating system, run antivirus, delete unused programs, defragment or clean up the disk, and back up files.
6. Crash and recovery: a crash is when the system stops working or freezes. Restart; use safe mode; restore from a backup or recovery software.

## Class activity

Pupils clean the keyboard and screen of a school computer, with the teacher's supervision, and fill in a maintenance checklist.

## Evaluation

1. State two precautions before cleaning a computer.
2. What is a backup and why is it important after a crash?

## Assignment

Complete the worksheet and the quiz on the app.

# Maintenance of the computer

## Why maintain a computer?

A computer in a school ICT room works in dust, heat and unstable power. Without care it slows down, overheats and loses data. **Maintenance** is the work done to keep it in good working order.

- **Preventive maintenance** is done regularly to stop faults: cleaning, updates, backups.
- **Corrective maintenance** is done after a fault, to repair or replace what is damaged.

## General cleaning

1. Switch off and **unplug** the computer.
2. Dust the case and vents with a **soft brush** or air blower.
3. Wipe the screen with a soft cloth that is only slightly damp. Never spray liquid on the screen or keyboard.
4. Clean the keyboard with an air blower and turn it upside down to shake out crumbs.
5. Keep the room cool and free of dust; no food or drinks.

## Batteries and the UPS

A laptop battery should be charged before it is fully empty and not left at full charge at all times in heat. Replace it when it no longer holds a charge or swells. A **UPS (uninterruptible power supply)** keeps the computer running for a few minutes during a power cut so that you can save and shut down properly. Its battery usually needs replacing after three to five years.

## Cleaning a DVD drive

Dust on the **lens** stops the drive reading discs. Use a **lens cleaning disc**, which has tiny brushes that sweep the lens as it spins.

## Hardware and software maintenance

*Hardware:* check that cables are tight; clean the cooling fan; check the power supply; do not move a computer while it is on.

*Software:* install updates of the operating system; run **antivirus** scans; remove programs you do not use; clear temporary files and free disk space; and make regular **backups**.

## Computer crash and data recovery

A **crash** is when the computer freezes or stops working. Causes include a virus, a power surge, overheating, a faulty hard disk and corrupted files. To recover: restart; start in **safe mode**; restore the system to an earlier point; or use **recovery software** to find lost files. The best protection is a **backup**, a copy of your important files on a flash drive, an external disk or online storage.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. define computer ethics and explain why it matters;
2. state the rules of the computer room and how it should be managed;
3. describe responsible ways of using a computer and the Internet;
4. describe ways of securing a computer and data.

## Materials

A poster of ICT room rules, a log book, a sample login screen, a list of scenarios (copying a classmate's project, downloading pirated music, using someone's password).

## Starter (5 minutes)

Read a scenario: a pupil finds a classmate's logged-in account on a school computer and posts a joke in his name. Ask: was it wrong? Why? Use it to introduce ethics.

## Development

1. Define ethics as the rules of right and wrong; computer ethics is the code of conduct for the use of computers and information. Reasons: protecting people's rights, privacy, work and property.
2. Computer room management: a log book, a timetable, a duty prefect, a first aid box, and a fire extinguisher; only authorised persons; keep the room clean.
3. Laboratory rules: no food or drink, no bags near computers, do not change settings or unplug cables, no personal flash drives without a virus scan, report faults, log out, and shut down properly.
4. Responsible use: do not copy software without a licence (piracy); do not plagiarise; respect others' privacy; do not spread viruses or false news; do not use another person's account.
5. Securing computers: passwords, locking the room, antivirus, backups, keeping software updated, and restricting user accounts.

## Class activity

Groups write ten ICT room rules, then judge four scenarios as ethical or unethical.

## Evaluation

1. Why should a food and drink ban apply in the computer room?
2. Give two examples of unethical use of a computer.

reading.content:
# Computer ethics and laboratory rules

## What is computer ethics?

**Ethics** is the set of rules that tell us what is right and what is wrong. **Computer ethics** is the code of good behaviour in using computers and information. It protects people's **privacy**, **property** and **rights** and keeps the computer room safe.

## Managing the computer room

- Keep a **log book** where each user writes name, date, computer number and time.
- Use a **timetable** so that every class has a turn.
- Allow only authorised persons and staff to use the room.
- Keep the room clean, cool and dust-free; have a **fire extinguisher** and **first aid box**.
- Keep a record of equipment and report faults to the ICT teacher.

## Laboratory rules

1. No food or drink: spills damage keyboards and crumbs attract insects.
2. No bags, wet hands or running about in the room.
3. Do not unplug cables or change the computer settings.
4. Scan every flash drive for viruses before using it.
5. Do not install programs without permission.
6. Log in with your own account and **log out** when you finish.
7. Shut down the computer properly, and push in the chair.
8. Report faults and accidents at once.

## Responsible use of computers

- Do not copy and sell software or films: this is **piracy**, a crime.
- Do not **plagiarise**: do not present others' work as yours; say where you got the information.
- Do not read others' files or use their passwords: respect **privacy**.
- Do not spread viruses, rumours or false news.
- Do not use the Internet to insult or threaten anybody.

## Securing computers and data

- Use **strong passwords** and change them often.
- Lock the computer room, and put important computers on a **UPS** and burglar-proof doors.
- Install **antivirus** and a **firewall** and keep software updated.
- Make regular **backups**.
- Give each user a limited **user account** so that only the administrator can change settings.

# Safety measures in the computer room

## Why safety matters

Long hours at a computer can cause **eye strain**, **backache**, **neck pain** and **repetitive strain injury (RSI)** in the wrists. Poor arrangement of a room can damage equipment, cause electric shock and even fire.

## Sitting arrangement

- Sit with the **back straight** and supported by the chair.
- Keep both **feet flat** on the floor or a footrest.
- Let the **thighs** be level and the **elbows bent at about 90 degrees**.
- Keep the **forearms level** with the keyboard and the **wrists straight**.

## Positioning the devices

- **Monitor**: directly in front, an arm's length away (about 50 to 70 cm), with the top of the screen at or just below eye level so the neck is not tilted.
- **Keyboard and mouse**: at elbow height, close to the body, with space to rest the wrists.
- **CPU (system unit)**: placed on a stand, not on the floor where dust and water reach it, with the air vents free of obstruction.
- **Peripheral devices** such as the printer and speaker: placed where cables do not cross the walkway.
- **Cables**: tied or put in trunking so that nobody trips over them.

## Lighting, dust and liquids

- Light the room well but avoid **glare** on the screen. Windows should be at the side, not behind or in front of the screen.
- Keep a **dust-free** environment: wipe surfaces, use covers and keep windows closed during harmattan dust.
- Keep **liquids and food away**. Spills damage keyboards and can cause electric shock.
- Keep the room cool and ventilated so the machines do not overheat.

## Electrical and fire safety

- Do not plug too many devices into one socket (**overloading**).
- Use a **surge protector** or UPS.
- Do not touch plugs or cables with wet hands; switch off before you plug or unplug.
- Report damaged cables.
- Have a **fire extinguisher** and know the exit. In a fire, switch off the power at the mains if it is safe, and leave the room calmly.

## Healthy habits

Look away from the screen for a few seconds every 20 to 30 minutes, blink often, stand up and stretch, and do not sit in one position for long periods.

# Careers in data processing and computer professional bodies

## Careers in computing

Computers have created many kinds of work. Some of the main ones are:

- **Data entry clerk**: types raw data, such as records and forms, into the computer accurately.
- **Computer operator**: runs the computers and checks that jobs are completed.
- **Programmer (software developer)**: writes the programs that tell computers what to do.
- **Systems analyst**: studies how an organisation works and designs a computer system to solve its problems.
- **Database administrator (DBA)**: designs, protects and manages databases.
- **Network administrator**: sets up and looks after the computer network.
- **Web designer**: builds and updates websites.
- **Computer engineer or technician**: repairs and maintains the hardware.
- **Cyber security officer**: guards systems and data against hackers.
- **Data analyst**: studies data to find patterns that help decisions.
- **ICT teacher**: teaches computer skills.

## Qualities of a good data processing professional

- **Accuracy** and attention to detail, because one wrong digit can change a result.
- **Honesty and confidentiality**: keeping private information such as results and salaries secret.
- **Patience** and discipline for long, careful work.
- **Willingness to keep learning**, because technology changes fast.
- **Teamwork** and good communication.
- **Problem-solving** skills.

## Computer professional bodies

A **professional body** is an association of people in the same profession that sets standards and protects the public.

- The **Computer Professionals Registration Council of Nigeria (CPN)** is the body set up by law to regulate the computing profession. It registers practitioners and companies, sets standards, and can take action against unregistered or unethical practice.
- The **Nigeria Computer Society (NCS)** is the professional association of computer practitioners. It promotes the profession, organises conferences and training, and encourages high standards among its members.

## Duties of professional bodies

They set a **code of conduct**, **register and certify** members, **train and update** them, **discipline** members who break the rules, and **represent** the profession in dealings with government and the public.

## Pathways

A learner can start with an SS3 certificate in Data Processing, then take a diploma or degree in computer science or information technology, or short professional certificates in networking, databases or cyber security.

# Computer viruses

## What is a computer virus?

A **computer virus** is a harmful program that copies itself and spreads from one file or computer to another without the user's knowledge, often damaging data and programs. Like a biological virus, it needs a host (a file or program) to spread.

## Types and examples of malicious programs

- **Boot sector virus**: infects the start-up area of a disk, so that the computer may not start.
- **File infector virus**: attaches to program files and spreads when they are run.
- **Macro virus**: hides in documents such as Word or Excel files and runs when the document is opened.
- **Worm**: spreads over a network by itself, slowing it down.
- **Trojan horse**: pretends to be a useful program but opens the way for attackers.
- **Ransomware**: locks your files and demands money to unlock them.

## Sources of virus infection

- Infected **flash drives** and other storage devices.
- **Email attachments** from unknown senders.
- **Pirated software** and cracked programs.
- **Unsafe websites** and downloads.
- Unprotected **networks**.

## Signs of a virus

The computer becomes **slow**; strange **messages** or pictures appear; programs **open or close by themselves**; files **disappear** or cannot open; the computer **crashes** or restarts often; the disk light flashes though you are doing nothing.

## Prevention, detection and deletion

**Prevention:** install **antivirus** software and keep it **updated** so that it knows new viruses; scan every flash drive before use; do not open attachments from strangers; avoid pirated software; use a **firewall**; keep the operating system updated; and make **backups**.

**Detection:** run a full **antivirus scan**.

**Deletion:** let the antivirus **quarantine** (isolate) or **delete** infected files; remove a bad program; if the system is badly damaged, reinstall it and restore files from a backup.

## Destructive effects

A virus can **delete or corrupt files**, **slow** the computer, **steal passwords** and personal information, **crash** the system, spread to other computers on the network and cost the school money for repair.

reading.content:
# The relational model: keys, relationships, queries and SQL

## The relational model

In a **relational database** data is stored in several **tables** that are linked. This avoids repeating data. Imagine writing a class's room and teacher beside every pupil's name; instead we keep this once in a Classes table and link it.

- An **entity** is something we keep data about, such as a student or a class.
- An **attribute** is a fact about an entity, such as a student's name. Attributes become the **fields** of the table.
- A **relationship** is a link between entities. One class has many students: a **one-to-many** relationship.

## Keys

The **primary key** uniquely identifies each record in its own table. The **foreign key** is a field in one table that holds the primary key of another table, making the link.

**Classes**

| ClassID | ClassName | Teacher |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SS3A | SS3A Data Processing | Mrs Eze |
| SS3B | SS3B Data Processing | Mr Bello |

**Students**

| AdmNo | Name | ClassID |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 001 | Ada Obi | SS3A |
| 002 | Musa Bello | SS3B |
| 003 | Tolu Ade | SS3A |

In Classes the primary key is **ClassID**. In Students the primary key is **AdmNo** and **ClassID** is the **foreign key**. It links each student to a class, so Tolu Ade's teacher can be found without repeating it.

## Forms, queries and reports

- A **form** is a screen for entering or viewing one record at a time.
- A **query** asks the database a question and returns the matching records.
- A **report** is a neat printed or displayed summary of data.

## Query languages

**Query by example (QBE)**: you fill in a grid: choose the table, the field to show and type the condition ('SS3A') under the ClassID field.

**SQL (Structured Query Language)**: you type commands.

- `SELECT * FROM Students;` shows every field of every record in Students.
- `SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE ClassID = 'SS3A';` shows the names of the pupils in SS3A: Ada Obi and Tolu Ade.
- `SELECT Name FROM Students ORDER BY Name;` lists names in alphabetical order.

SELECT chooses fields, FROM names the table and WHERE gives the condition.

reading.content:
# File organisation

## Terms

- A **field** is one item of data, such as a name.
- A **record** is a set of related fields about one item, such as a pupil's AdmNo, Name and Class.
- A **file** is a collection of records of the same kind, such as the file of all pupils.
- A **key field** is the field that identifies a record, such as AdmNo.

**File organisation** is the way the records are arranged and stored in a file. The choice affects how quickly records can be found and processed.

## Types of file organisation

**1. Serial organisation.** Records are stored one after the other in the order in which they arrive, with no sorting. To find a record, the computer must read from the beginning. It is simple and cheap and used for logs and temporary transaction files, such as a list of the day's sales.

**2. Sequential organisation.** Records are stored in order of a **key field**, for example from the smallest admission number to the largest. It is quick to process all the records in turn, as in a monthly payroll. To add a record the file must be rewritten, and finding one record still needs a search from the top.

**3. Indexed sequential organisation.** Records are kept in key order and there is also an **index**, a small table that tells where blocks of records are found, like the index of a textbook. A single record is found quickly through the index, and all records can still be read in order. It is used in library catalogues and school records.

**4. Random (direct access) organisation.** The position of each record is worked out from its key by a formula, so the record is found directly, however big the file is. It is the fastest for single records but needs a disk (not tape) and is more costly to set up. It is used in ATMs and airline booking systems, where a customer's record must appear at once.

## Comparing them

| Organisation | Finding one record | Processing all records | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Serial | slowest | slow | transaction log |
| Sequential | slow | fast | payroll |
| Indexed sequential | fast | fast | library catalogue |
| Random | fastest | not in order | ATM, bookings |

## Choosing

If every record is processed each time, as in payroll, sequential is good. If single records are looked up quickly, as with a customer at an ATM, use random access. If both are needed, use indexed sequential.

# Database security and the database administrator

## Why secure data?

A database may hold results, fees, salaries, medical records and bank accounts. If it is changed, stolen or lost, people can suffer. **Data security** is protecting data from **unauthorised access**, **change**, **loss** and **theft**.

Threats include hackers, viruses, dishonest or careless staff, fire and theft of computers, and power failure.

## Access control

**Access control** decides who may use the database and what they may do.

- **User name and password** (authentication): the user proves who he is.
- **Levels of access**: a pupil may have **read only** access to his own result; a teacher may **read and write** the scores of his class; only the administrator has **full control** to create, delete and change the structure.
- **Physical control**: a locked server room and burglar-proof doors.
- **Audit log**: a record of who opened or changed which data and when.

## Data encryption

**Encryption** scrambles data into an unreadable form called **ciphertext** using a **key**, so that anyone who steals it cannot read it. **Decryption** turns it back into **plaintext** with the key.

A very simple method is the **Caesar cipher**: shift each letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. With a shift of 3, A becomes D, B becomes E, C becomes F and so on. The word CAT becomes **FDW**, and BAD becomes **EDG**. Real systems use much stronger methods, such as those that protect bank transfers and WhatsApp messages.

## Other protection

Make regular **backups**; keep **antivirus** and a **firewall**; update software; and plan how to recover from a disaster.

## The database administrator (DBA)

The **database administrator** is the person responsible for the database. The DBA:

- creates users and gives each the right level of access;
- protects the data with passwords, encryption and a firewall;
- makes **backups** and restores data when lost;
- monitors performance and fixes faults;
- decides the structure of the database and keeps it organised.
